newsitem.title: USA: POLL--No U.S. rate hike seen at Fed's Aug 19 meet.
newsitem.headline: POLL--No U.S. rate hike seen at Fed's Aug 19 meet.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is not expected to raise the 5.50-percent federal funds rate when its policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on August 19, economists in a Reuters poll unanimously said.

All 33 experts polled by Reuters cited the combination of low inflation and healthy growth as the factors precluding a move by the U.S. central bank on the two interest rates it controls -- fed funds and the discount rate.
However, two-thirds of the analysts predicted the Fed will have to tighten credit at least once before year end.
"The economy is going to be growing, probably between 2.0 to 2.5 percent over the foreseeable future," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.
"That's what the Fed wants, that's what the Fed is expecting, that's what we're looking for, and that should leave policy unchanged," Schaja said.
The FOMC last raised the funds rate by 25 basis points on March 25. The Fed last moved on the discount rate in January 1996, lowering it by 25 basis points to 5.00 percent.
Philip Braverman, senior vice president and chief economist at DKB Securities, agreed there is no urgency for a rate move this month.
"We are not anywhere nearly as vulnerable as we once were to a pick up of inflation," said Braverman.
However, the DKB economist cautioned that the Fed, like many market participants, remained alert for signs the economy may be growing too fast, fueling inflationary pressures.
Such concern led 24 out of the 33 economists polled by Reuters to predict the Fed would raise the funds rate by 25 to 50 basis points later this year.
Among these, six expected the FOMC to nudge up the funds rate by 25 basis points as early as its September 30 meeting.
"The Fed will respond with one more insurance move to strength in the second half of the year," said John Ryding, managing director and senior economist at Bear Stearns and Co.
But Ryding did not expect that "insurance" to be taken on evidence of "a sufficiently strong economy for a sufficiently long period of time," until November.
FOMC meetings are scheduled for September 30, November 12, and December 16. The Fed's Beige Book on economic conditions, used for discussions at the FOMC, is due for release Wednesday.
